documents.title: VigiBase WHO global database of individual case safety reports

chunks.content: Key Points Introduction Cytokines play a central role in the development and treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, with many signaling through the Janus kinase/signal transducers and activators of transcription (JAK/STAT) pathway [ ]. JAK inhibitors are indicated for a variety of inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, with approvals for diseases such as spondyloarthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, atopic dermatitis and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) [ , ]. RA as a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease affects 1% of the global population [ ]. Patients with RA exhibit osteoporosis as a frequent co-morbidity, which increases the risk of bone fractures [ ]. Osteoporosis and fractures lead to a significant reduction in functional impairment and a decreased quality of life for patients [ , ]. The initial treatment involves glucocorticoids and non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), followed by synthetic disease modifying drugs (sDMARDs) and biologic disease modifying drugs (bDMARDs) as secondary options [ , ]. Especially glucocorticoids and NSAIDs have shown associations with increased fracture risks in this already vulnerable population [ , ]. JAK inhibitors specifically target the JAK/STAT pathway by inhibiting one or more intracellular tyrosine kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2) and block cytokine signalling [ , ]. Tofacitinib was the first substance in class approved for the treatment of RA by the US Food and Drug Association (FDAs) in 2012. Other JAK inhibitors were approved by FDA/European Medicines Agency (EMA) for RA [ ]. The JAK inhibitor abrocitinib was recently approved for atopic dermatitis, but not for the treatment of RA [ ]. While the primary pharmacological action of JAK inhibitors involves cytokine-signalling inhibition, recent studies have shown additional effects. Tofacitinib and baricitinib exhibit direct positive effects on bone synthesis and osteoblast function in murine models, without directly affecting osteoclasts [ ]. The European Medicines Agency endorsed a recent update to the summary of product characteristics (SmPC) for tofacitinib, introducing a warning about an increased fracture risk [ , ]. In September 2022 the SmPC for tofacitinib was updated to include this new adverse drug reaction [ ]. Due to the paucity of data and clinical studies with controversial outcomes [ – ], the objective of the current study was to analyze the real-world reports on bone fractures in association with the JAK inhibitors tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib and abrocitinib, which were previously assessed in an EMA referral on an increased risk of cancer and major cardiovascular events [ ]. This study was designed to assess time-trends of reports, patient demographics, and disproportionality of fracture for approved JAK inhibitors to assess a potential class effect and contribute to gain insights on the ongoing discussion on the safety profile of JAK inhibitors in clinical practice. Methods Data Source Pharmacovigilance data were obtained from VigiBase, the WHO database of adverse drug reactions reporting, which is managed by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC) [ , ]. Since 1968, VigiBase has collected and processed worldwide adverse drug reactions (ADRs). These ADRs are reported as individual case safety reports (ICSRs) by more than 140 countries. Over 30 million reports have been obtained from healthcare professionals, patients and pharmaceutical companies. The ICSRs contain information about sex, age, country, reactions and medications that can be associated with the reported ADR. The reports vary in completeness, and the likelihood of establishing a causal association is not uniform across all entries. All potential ADRs within VigiBase are documented and categorized using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA ® ) version 25.1. Data Extraction and Outcomes This study included ICSRs reporting active ingredients of tofacitinib, upadacitinib, baricitinib, filgotinib and abrocitinib as suspect or interacting drugs focusing on JAK inhibitors for chronic inflammatory disorders that were included in the EMA referral in October 2022. The data extraction was with the dataset date of on 14 March 2023. The comparator group for disproportionality were all other reports in VigiBase during the same period as the JAK inhibitors. The primary outcome of interest in this study was reporting of bone fractures. Bone fractures were identified by the MedDRA ® High-Level Group Term (MedDRA ® HLGT) “Fracture”. Avulsion fractures and tooth fractures were omitted from the analysis, as they were not classified as typical bone fractures. The full list of fractures identified in the analysis is listed in supplementary table . Data Analysis The demographics of the ICSRs were tabulated using counts and proportions or means and standard deviations (SD) for each individual JAK inhibitor. The ICSRs were stratified by the JAK inhibitor active ingredient and the primary outcome (bone fracture). ICSRs listing more than one JAK inhibitor as suspect or interacting were treated as separate reports. Co-medications were grouped and identified in the VigiBase database. ICSRs with more than one of the same comedication group was counted as a single entry. ICSRs with a recorded age equal to 0 months and without any

Data Analysis The demographics of the ICSRs were tabulated using counts and proportions or means and standard deviations (SD) for each individual JAK inhibitor. The ICSRs were stratified by the JAK inhibitor active ingredient and the primary outcome (bone fracture). ICSRs listing more than one JAK inhibitor as suspect or interacting were treated as separate reports. Co-medications were grouped and identified in the VigiBase database. ICSRs with more than one of the same comedication group was counted as a single entry. ICSRs with a recorded age equal to 0 months and without any other hint of transplacental administration were set to age “unknown”. A disproportionality analysis was conducted using the ROR along with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) [ ]. The RORs were calculated for each individual JAK inhibitor as well as for the overall reports within VigiBase. This disproportionality method aims to compare the observed versus the expected reporting ratio for an specific event and a medicinal product [ ]. Disproportionality analyses were performed to examine the outcome of interest, and the expected reporting ratio was determined by considering the ICSRs of all medications in VigiBase, except the ones under investigation. In a secondary analysis, we examined age and gender as potential confounders. Disproportionality was assessed for females and males, and ROR was calculated for adults aged ≥ 75 years. To address confounding, we used TNF-alpha inhibitors (ATC code L04AB tumor necrosis factor alpha [TNF- alpha] inhibitors) as an alternative comparator group and repeated the disproportionality analyses. We complied to the READUS-PV guidelines on the reporting of a disproportionality analysis for drug safety signal detection using individual case safety reports in pharmacovigilance [ ]. A time series analysis was conducted for all reports of each JAK inhibitor as well as for the overall reporting covering the period from the first quarter of 2014 to the first quarter of 2023. The analyses included both fracture-specific ICSRs and overall ICSRs. The cut-off date for the analysis was set at 13 September 2022, marking the date of the EMA updated the tofacitinib SmPC. This cut-off line was employed to delineate a distinct period in the analysis corresponding to the regulatory update. All analyses were executed using the statistical software R (version 4.2.2), ensuring a robust and standardized approach to the examination of the temporal patterns in reported fracture cases associated with JAK inhibitors. This time series analysis serves to elucidate trends, potential fluctuations, and noteworthy patterns in the reporting frequency of fractures over the specified period. Results Demographics Table provides a comprehensive overview of the demographic characteristics extracted from 165,619 ICSRs overall and stratified by the five JAK inhibitors: tofacitinib ( n = 122,037), upadacitinib ( n = 27,786), bariticinib ( n = 14,616), filgotinib (830) and abrocitinib ( n = 350). Overall, female patients accounted for the majority of patients (76.2%) and the mean age was 59.1 years (SD 13.9). Most of the reports originated from North America (77.3%) followed by Europe (14.5%). The reporting peak was observed in 2022 (21.8%) succeeded by 2021 (15.9%) and 2019 (15.4%). RA was the predominant reported indication (51.9%), with the exception of abrocitinib reports. The most frequently overall reported comedication of interest for all ICSRs was sDMARDS (14.9%), followed by NSAIDs (7.8%) and glucocorticoids (7.1%). A list of the specific comedication can be found in Supplementary Table . The mean number of medications per patient was 2.4 (SD 3.3) and most patients reported using 0–4 total number of medications (87.1%). Among all ICSRs, 2987 (1.8%) documented bone fracture as an ADR, with tofacitinib having 2198 (1.8%), upadacitinib 634 (2.3%), baricitinib 144 (1.0%), filgotinib 10 (1.2%) and abrocitinib 1 (0.3%), respectively (Table ). A range of 38 different bone fractures were reported, with hip fractures (12.3%), upper limp fractures (10.7%) and lower limb fractures (8.8%) being the most frequently documented (Supplementary Table 1). ICSRs with bone fractures reported as an ADR showed a higher proportion of female gender (87.8% versus 76.2%) older average age (66.3 versus 59.1 years), compared with the patients without reported fracture, respectively. Elderly patients (> 65 years) were more common in the fracture reports (49.5%) compared with overall reports (29.1%). Comedication usage was higher in patients with fractures than without (mean 3.6 versus 2.4 drugs), while sDMARDs (23.4%), NSAIDs (13.8%) and glucocorticoids (12.6%) were the most frequently reported drug classes. These trends were consistent across all JAK inhibitors. Disproportionate Analysis Figure illustrates the result of the disproportionate analysis (also Supplementary Table ). The overall ROR for all JAK inhibitors was 3.35 (95% CI 3.23–3.48) with a similar ROR being observed for tofacitinib (3.34, 95% CI 3.20–3.48). Upadacitinib exhibited the highest ROR of 4.23 (95% CI 3.80–4.57), while baricitinib demonstrated the lowest ROR of 1.80 (95% CI 1.52–2.11). The ROR for filgotinib was 2.24 (95%

in patients with fractures than without (mean 3.6 versus 2.4 drugs), while sDMARDs (23.4%), NSAIDs (13.8%) and glucocorticoids (12.6%) were the most frequently reported drug classes. These trends were consistent across all JAK inhibitors. Disproportionate Analysis Figure illustrates the result of the disproportionate analysis (also Supplementary Table ). The overall ROR for all JAK inhibitors was 3.35 (95% CI 3.23–3.48) with a similar ROR being observed for tofacitinib (3.34, 95% CI 3.20–3.48). Upadacitinib exhibited the highest ROR of 4.23 (95% CI 3.80–4.57), while baricitinib demonstrated the lowest ROR of 1.80 (95% CI 1.52–2.11). The ROR for filgotinib was 2.24 (95% CI 1.11–3.94). Abrocitinib had one bone fracture reported and no disproportionate analysis was conducted due to the low reporting. All the calculated RORs were statistically significant and had p values below 0.05. In patients with baricitinib, the proportion of those using NSAID or corticosteroid was similar between those with fractures and those without fractures. In secondary analyses focusing on age and gender (Supplementary Table ), significant results were consistent except for males in the baricitinib group. When TNF-alpha inhibitors were used as a comparator group, the overall ROR was also constistent; ROR 1.87 (1.80–1.95). Time Series Analysis Figure a and b illustrate the reporting trend over time, highlighting the SmPC update of tofacitinib as a vertical line. Figure a shows the overall reporting of cases related to JAK inhibitor use and Fig. b shows the reporting of fracture-related cases. Abrocitinib was not included in Fig. a and b due to low reporting. The time series analysis showed an increase in total and fracture-related reports especially for upadacitinib. The total reports for upadacitinib increased from 13,467 to 27,786 in 2022 Q3 to 2023 Q1 and reporting of fractures increased from 387 to 634 in the same period. For all JAK inhibitors, the total reporting and fractures-related reports increased after the tofacitinib SmPC update driven by tofacitinib and upadacitinib reports. For tofacitinib, a small increase in total ICSRs reported was observed; however, the reporting of ICSRs mentioning bone fractures did not increase after the SmPC update. No notable changes in reporting patterns were found for baricitinib and filgotinib after the update. The results from the full dataset used for the time series analysis are displayed in supplementary table . Discussion The findings of this real-world pharmacovigilance study elucidate a significant association between use of JAK-inhibitors and an increased reporting of bone fractures. Notably, the disproportionality analyses demonstrated elevated ROR with a safety signal for upadacitinib, tofacitinib and filgotinib, indicating a potential risk of bone fractures compared to other medications. The predominance of female patients and the higher average age in patients with fractures align with established osteoporosis risk factors. Co-medication usage, particularly with NSAIDs and glucocorticoids, is noteworthy in patients with reported fractures. The results support existing warnings for tofacitinib and raise concerns for other JAK inhibitors such as upadactinib, baricitinib and filgotinib. However, until now, a regulatory update has only been issued for tofacitinib so far. Among the JAK inhibitors, upadacitinib demonstrated the highest ROR; however, with limited existing real-world evidence for the other JAK inhibitors a potential class effect for JAK inhibitors cannot be ruled out based on the observed disproportionality. JAK inhibitors with selectivity for JAK1 and JAK2 can impede osteoclastogenesis by suppressing receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa beta (RANKL) expression [ ]. A small clinical study demonstrated that one year of treatment with tofacitinib led to a statistically significant increase in bone mineral density at the lumbar spine (4.6%, 95% CI 3.8–5.4%) and femoral neck (3.0%, 95% CI 2.2–3.8%), as well as a decrease in bone resorption markers [ ]. This indicates that the JAK inhibitors could have a positive effect on bone metabolism. The broad range of pharmacological effects, particularly affecting bone metabolism and the immune system, have raised new concerns about potential long-term adverse effects on bone metabolism, which may contribute to an increased incidence of bone fractures [ ]. These concerns and conflicting data have resulted in the SmPC for tofacitinib to be updated in September 2022 [ , ]. However, studies using bone fracture as the primary outcome are limited in literature and clinical evidence is sparse. A post-authorization study, using the WHO global pharmacovigilance database (VigiBase), presented secondary findings regarding the incidence rates of fractures for tofacitinib and baricitinib [ ]. The reported information component (IC 025 ) values were 1.6 for tofacitinib and 0.4 for baricitinib [ ]. A Korean study using spontaneous reports and online patient reviews found an overall reporting odds ratio (ROR) of 1.49 (95% CI 1.03–2.14) for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib [ ]. However, these findings were secondary and not a specific focus in the articles [ , ]. The results obtained from our study comply with results from these published real-world studies, although they did not

global pharmacovigilance database (VigiBase), presented secondary findings regarding the incidence rates of fractures for tofacitinib and baricitinib [ ]. The reported information component (IC 025 ) values were 1.6 for tofacitinib and 0.4 for baricitinib [ ]. A Korean study using spontaneous reports and online patient reviews found an overall reporting odds ratio (ROR) of 1.49 (95% CI 1.03–2.14) for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib [ ]. However, these findings were secondary and not a specific focus in the articles [ , ]. The results obtained from our study comply with results from these published real-world studies, although they did not focus on fractures as an adverse event related to JAK inhibitor use and potential risk factors for bone fractures [ , ]. The study by Hoisnard et al. used data from 126,815 ICSRs associated with JAK inhibitors and found a 1.7% occurrence of fractures, which closely aligns with our findings of 1.8% [ ]. In the study by Hoisnard et al., tofacitinib exhibited a higher IC 025 compared with baricitinib, a trend that our disproportionate analysis also supports. The Korean study using spontaneous reports and online patient reviews from the USA and Korea, reported an odds ratio of 1.49 (95% CI 1.03–2.14) for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib, which is lower than our findings [ ]. This disparity in results can be attributed to the differences in data collection sources. Patient reviews, while valuable, can vary in terms of accuracy, completeness and reliability [ ]. Findings from these two real-world studies consistently demonstrated a potential class effect for JAK inhibitors on bone fractures, which aligns with the findings of our current study. In 2022, the EMA and Swissmedic issued recommendations to minimize serious side effects associated with Janus kinase inhibitors, including thromboembolism, malignancy and infections [ , ]. The ORAL Surveillance study indicated higher risks of cancer and major cardiovascular events with tofacitinib. The increased fracture risk also refers to this study, although these results are not included in the published trial. The significance of considering risk factors in the latest SmPC update for tofacitinib advises cautious use in patients with known factors predisposing to fractures, including elderly individuals, females and those undergoing corticosteroid therapy, irrespective of indication and dosage [ ]. The EMA and Swissmedic are regulatory bodies that issued a safety warning regarding bone fractures associated with use of the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib. While the warning specifically applies to tofacitinib, our results indicate potential association of bone fractures for other JAK inhibitors with a potential class effect. The duration of drug exposure may affect the risk of fractures, such as the development of osteoporosis. This might also be reflected in the length of market use among different substances within the JAK inhibitor class, with tofacitinib being the oldest. Future studies should also consider including newer JAK inhibitors such as decernotinib, peficitinib, itacitinib, delgocitinib and gusacitinib to provide a more comprehensive understanding of this class of drugs. Another observation was the higher ROR for upadacitinib compared with other JAK inhibitors. Upadacitinib and filgotinib are JAK1 selective inhibitors, while tofacitinib is non-specific and baricitinib is selective for JAK1 and JAK2 [ ]. An in vitro study concluded that inhibition of JAK1/2 receptors suppressed RANKL-expression and inhibited development of osteoclast, leading a decrease in bone desorption [ ]. In vivo data from knockout mice with inflammatory bone destruction showed that treatment with the JAK1-speific inhibitor, ABT-318, blocked bone destruction by targeting mature osteoclasts [ ]. Findings from in vivo/in vitro experiments indicate a preventive effect on bone destruction; however, our findings are not in line with the experimental data. A hypothesis for the occurrence of bone fractures associated with JAK inhibitor use is the inhibition of cytokines. Cytokines and interleukins (ILs), such as IL-3, IL-6 and IL-17, have a key role in maintaining bone formation and upregulates osteoblast genesis, leading to an increase in bone formation [ – ]. These cytokines are regulated by JAK1/JAK2 receptors and inhibition will result in production of less cytokines. This could potentially disturb the bone remodeling balance and lead to increased bone resorption. Inhibition of JAK receptors will have extensive effects on bone metabolism and cytokine signaling, which can lead to an increased fracture risk. However, more studies are needed to confirm the effect of JAK selectivity and cytokine inhibition on bone fracture risks. In secondary analyses using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator group, both tofacitibin and upadacitinib were associated with increased reporting of fractures (ROR 1.82, 95% CI 1.74–1.91 for tofacitinib and 2.23, 95%CI: 2.06–2.42 for upadacitinib). This analysis suggests that the increased reporting of fractures with these drugs may not be solely attributed to comedication use, but rather to other factors such as drug-specific or class effects. Our results indicate increased reporting of bone fractures globally for tofacitinib, upadacitinib and baricitinib, suggesting a potential

more studies are needed to confirm the effect of JAK selectivity and cytokine inhibition on bone fracture risks. In secondary analyses using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator group, both tofacitibin and upadacitinib were associated with increased reporting of fractures (ROR 1.82, 95% CI 1.74–1.91 for tofacitinib and 2.23, 95%CI: 2.06–2.42 for upadacitinib). This analysis suggests that the increased reporting of fractures with these drugs may not be solely attributed to comedication use, but rather to other factors such as drug-specific or class effects. Our results indicate increased reporting of bone fractures globally for tofacitinib, upadacitinib and baricitinib, suggesting a potential class effect. The potential mechanism could be associated with cytokine signaling inhibition and direct effects on bone metabolism. Our findings propose further evaluation and potential adjustments of the SmPCs of other JAK inhibitors. Limitations The present study has certain limitations, particularly concerning the database and source of reporting. It should be noted that spontaneous reporting is not suitable for estimating the prevalence or incidence of adverse events among patients exposed to drugs [ ]. Another significant limitation is the lack of case-causality assessment. Individual case safety reports may not provide conclusive evidence of a causal association due to the absence of information on potential alternative causes and incomplete data regarding the timing of adverse events [ ]. The information comes from a variety of sources, and the probability that the suspected adverse effect is drug-related is not the same in all cases [ ]. Baricitinib was the first JAK inhibitor licensed in Europe in both the 2 mg and 4 mg formulation, but only the 2 mg formulation was approved by the FDA due to safety concerns. It is not clear, if there is a dose-dependence of the reaction, but this may explain the higher reporting rates from this region. While treatment guidelines for rheumatoid arthritis and management of comorbidities such as osteoporosis are broadly aligned between Europe and the USA, there may still be regional differences in co-medication practices, treatment duration, or dosage that could influence fracture risk [ , ]. However, due to the limitations of the current pharmacovigilance dataset, we are unable to perform a detailed analysis of these potential regional variations. ICSRs reported to VigiBase doubled for upadacitinib between 2022 Q3 and 2023 Q1, while reporting for other JAK inhibitors remained stable. This increase resulted in a surge in reported bone fractures compared to other approved JAK inhibitors. The cause for this rise is not clear, but increased regulatory communication and approval of new indications could be factors [ , ]. In 2022, the EMA and Swissmedic issued recommendations to minimize serious side effects associated with Janus kinase inhibitors, including thromboembolism, malignancy and infections [ , ]. An alert concerning a drug adverse reaction may also lead to a “ripple effect”, resulting in an increase in reports of the adverse reaction with other drugs in the same pharmacological or therapeutic class as the drug initially flagged in the alert [ ]. This phenomenon should be considered when interpreting the increased reporting of adverse reactions, as it may not be limited to a single drug but affect others within the class as well. The present work is subject to other study-specific limitations that should be acknowledged. One limitation is specific to the availability of data for filgotinib and abrocitinib. The sparse number of reported cases for these drugs constrained the ability to conduct comprehensive analyses. Furthermore, the low number of reports for abrocitinib prevented a disproportionate analysis. Another significant limitation concerns the selected outcome of interest, namely bone fractures. Unlike immediate adverse events, the occurrence of a bone fracture is a complex outcome that does not directly establish a causal link to the administered drug within the database [ ]. Bone fractures are influenced by many factors, including mechanistic stress, which may not be linked to the use of JAK inhibitors or other reported comedication [ ]. Rheumatoid arthritis is a known risk factor for fractures [ , ]. In our analysis, we observed a higher proportion of patients with RA among those using upadacitinib compared with tofacitinib. This difference in the proportion of patients with RA may contribute to the observed variation in fracture risk. We acknowledge that this factor could influence our findings, and we recommend conducting sensitivity analyses in future studies to account for the impact of RA and other relevant variables. The risk of fracture is increased with long-term use of drugs such as oral glucocorticoids or NSAIDs. Due to limitations in data availability and technical constraints, we could not adjust for concurrent medication or specific indications. Nevertheless, using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator yielded comparable results (ROR 1.87, 95% CI 1.80–1.95). Future studies with real-world data should further investigate the impact of co-medication and indication on fracture risk in patients using JAK

The risk of fracture is increased with long-term use of drugs such as oral glucocorticoids or NSAIDs. Due to limitations in data availability and technical constraints, we could not adjust for concurrent medication or specific indications. Nevertheless, using TNF-alpha inhibitors as a comparator yielded comparable results (ROR 1.87, 95% CI 1.80–1.95). Future studies with real-world data should further investigate the impact of co-medication and indication on fracture risk in patients using JAK inhibitors. Despite these limitations, our analysis adjusted for other potential confounding factors such as age and gender, were consistent with the primary findings. It is important to interpret the findings of this study considering these limitations, as they affect the generalizability and conclusive determination of causality. Despite these limitations, the utilization of pharmacovigilance analyses, such as disproportionality analysis, remains a valuable method for identifying safety signals. The extensive global coverage of VigiBase, encompassing data from more than 140 countries, enhances the detection of adverse events related to JAK inhibitors [ ]. Pharmacovigilance data can support decision making for regulatory authorities and the utilization of spontaneous reporting is an effective approach for monitoring the safety profile of medications throughout their lifespan. Conclusion Results obtained from this real-world pharmacovigilance study add to the ongoing clinical and regulatory debate regarding the safety profile of JAK inhibitors. Patients with a bone fracture were mostly female, elderly and frequently reported use of medications associated with risks of bone fractures, such as glucocorticoids. Fracture reports have increased for tofacitinib, upadacitinib, baricitinib and filgotinib, suggesting a potential class effect on bone fracture among JAK inhibitors. However, cautious interpretation is required due to the nature of the data, which is subject to several limitations and biases. The association of fractures with older and female patients and concurrent medications may indicate an existing fracture risk. Although a safety update has been issued for tofacitinib in the European Union, our findings suggest the reassessment for warnings regarding other JAK inhibitors. Real-world data specific to JAK inhibitors and bone fractures is scarce, highlighting the importance of further assessment to establish a conclusive causal relationship, particularly for filgotinib and abrocitinib, where additional data is required to evaluate their impact on bone fractures. documents.title: WHO Pharmacovigilance Method Reviews technical guidance

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Polio has been a public health threat since the 20th century. It is a highly infectious viral disease with severe complications and is prone to outbreaks [ , ]. Polio primarily affects children, with symptoms including low fever, sore throat, severe limb pain, flaccid paralysis, limb deformities and permanent disability [ , ]. A sore throat and low fever are the hallmarks of the clinical symptoms in most cases, which often go away in less than a week [ ]. Paralytic polio occurs in <1% of infections; it can be permanent and present 12 months after onset [ ], with 5–10% of paralytic polio cases resulting in death [ , , ]. Paralytic polio cases reached epidemic levels in the 20th century, after the first outbreaks in Europe and the United States were reported in the 19th century [ , ]. Global estimates show that 12–20 million people have been impacted by the infection since the 19th century [ , ]. In 1988, the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) was launched after a resolution passed by the World Health Assembly, with over 350,000 children recorded as having paralytic polio across 125 countries [ ]. The GPEI’s goals are to detect and stop the spread of the poliovirus and strengthen immunization programs globally. Post-eradication strategies, such as sustaining high vaccination rates and strengthening surveillance efforts, are important in the goal of eradicating polio [ , ]. In 2014, as part of the GPEI, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended adding at least one dose of inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) to routine immunization schedules. This measure was proposed as a strategy to reduce the potential risk of re-emergence of type 2 polio after the Sabin type 2 strains have been removed from the oral polio vaccine (OPV) [ , , , ]. The GPEI Polio Eradication Strategy 2022–2026 set 2023 as a target year to interrupt all remaining type 1 wild poliovirus (WPV1) transmission (Goal One) and type 2 circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) transmission (Goal Two), with the aim of reaching eradication by 2026. From January 2021 to May 2023, only one of the three WPV serotypes, i.e., WPV1, was circulating in four countries: Afghanistan, Pakistan, Namibia and Mozambique [ ]. Currently, WPV1 remains endemic in Afghanistan and Pakistan [ , ], with a mutated variant form of paralytic polio, i.e., cVDPV, in 32 countries, including Nigeria [ , , , ]. In August 2024, the United Nations reported a case of paralytic polio in Gaza for the first time in the 25 years of its polio-free status, with conflict disrupting regular child vaccination programs [ , ]. The infection was linked to the type 2 variant detected earlier in environmental samples collected from Gaza wastewater, with poor sanitation resulting in poliovirus typically spreading through the fecal–oral route in unsanitary environments [ , , ]. While Nigeria, the seventh most populous country in the world, was declared free of WPV in 2020, the transmission of the circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVPV2) strain and eradication of all variant strains of polio remain a concern [ ]. As of August 2024, 30 cases of cVDPV have been reported in Nigeria, constituting 42% of the 72 cases of cVDPV reported globally, with the potential to amplify the transmission through a cross-border spread [ , ]. Nigeria has focused on the management of infectious diseases and outbreaks such as Ebola, Lassa fever and COVID-19 using the incident management approach with support provided by the Nigerian Ministry of Health, Nigerian Center for Disease Control, private sector and international community [ ]. Several interventions and policies have been established for the eradication of all forms of polio in Nigeria; for example, the 1999 National Program on Immunization (NPI) [ ], the National Primary Health Care Development Agency with support from the WHO to address the spread of cVDPV2 [ , ], the CORE Group Partners Project (CGPP) with the aid of the WHO, and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) focusing on the health and safety concerns of northern communities and improving polio vaccine acceptance [ , , ]. In February 2014, with WPV still being transmitted endemically in Pakistan, Afghanistan and Nigeria, the Nigerian health ministry introduced the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) into the nation’s routine immunization schedule to children 14 weeks to 59 months of age [ ]. However, vaccination services for polio in Nigeria fall short of the WHO’s target of 90% national coverage, as 2.3 million children in Nigeria have not received routine polio immunization, the second highest number in the world [ ]. These shortcomings resonate with wider routine immunization rates reporting that about 3.1 million Nigerian children (14% of global data) are estimated to be zero-dose or missed-dose, while children who are not vaccinated are at risk for vaccine-preventable

health ministry introduced the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) into the nation’s routine immunization schedule to children 14 weeks to 59 months of age [ ]. However, vaccination services for polio in Nigeria fall short of the WHO’s target of 90% national coverage, as 2.3 million children in Nigeria have not received routine polio immunization, the second highest number in the world [ ]. These shortcomings resonate with wider routine immunization rates reporting that about 3.1 million Nigerian children (14% of global data) are estimated to be zero-dose or missed-dose, while children who are not vaccinated are at risk for vaccine-preventable diseases such as polio [ , ]. Multiple reasons have been suggested for low or delayed polio vaccine uptake and challenges with polio eradication in Nigeria. A complex interplay of factors are involved, including misconceptions and misunderstanding about the polio vaccine, a boycott in Northern Nigeria and vaccine hesitancy, illiteracy, areas of conflict such as the Boko Haram insurgency, challenges in reaching underserved communities, failure of the cold-chain system and, more recently, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic that disrupted global polio vaccination campaigns [ , , , , , , ]. Overall, Nigeria’s health system is underdeveloped, with inadequate and outdated medical facilities and equipment and overall poor quality of care, especially in rural communities, which further increases health inequalities, limiting accessibility to services [ , , ]. Other problems include corruption, poor drug availability and challenges of affordability, as most patients in Nigeria obtain their medications through out-of-pocket costs [ , ]. Hence, there are fundamental weaknesses in Nigeria’s health system and healthcare indicators remain some of the lowest in Africa [ , , , ]. Vaccine delivery in Nigeria is overseen by the NPI [ , ], with all vaccines approved by the WHO and delivered by trained health workers either at health facilities or at remote outreach sites in communities. Six different vaccines have been employed to stop polio transmission and for the eradication of WPV in Nigeria: ▪ Oral polio vaccine (OPV), i.e., trivalent oral polio vaccine (tOPV), which contains Sabin strains of all three poliovirus serotypes (i.e., OPV 1, 2 and 3), was used against poliovirus types 1, 2, and 3 and led to the eradication of WPV type 2 (WPV2) in Nigeria—first eradicated in 2015, with over 379 million OPV doses administered throughout Nigeria in 2013 and at least 200 million doses in 2014 [ , ]. ▪ In April 2016, tOPV was withdrawn from routine vaccination coverage with the switch to bivalent oral polio vaccine (bOPV), which contains Sabin serotypes 1 and 3 strains (i.e., OPV1 and OPV3), protecting against poliovirus types 1 and 3 [ , ]. ▪ To phase out type 2 OPV and provide protection against poliovirus types 1, 2 and 3, Nigeria incorporated a single dose of inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) at 14 weeks of age into the regular vaccination schedule in 2015. ▪ Monovalent oral polio vaccines types 1-2-3 (mOPV1, mOPV2 and mOPV3) were introduced to protect against each individual type of poliovirus, respectively. However, there were continuous outbreaks of cVDPV2 persisting in Nigeria despite the 180 million doses of mOPV2 administered between 2018 and 2022 [ , ]. Between 2018 and 2022, 526 cases of cVDPV2 were detected in Nigeria with spread to other countries within Africa [ , ]. Supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) delivered 16 million full doses and 19 million fractional doses of IPV between 2017 and 2020 to support the monovalent oral polio vaccine type 2 (mOPV2) outbreak response campaigns and increase IPV coverage [ ]. By 2022, national coverage had grown from 42% at the time of commencement in 2015 to 62% in 2021, and a second IPV dosage was introduced at the age of six weeks [ , ]. ▪ In 2021, a novel oral poliovirus vaccine type 2 (nOPV2) was introduced, as Nigeria became the first country to be approved by the Global nOPV2 Advisory Group to use the more genetically stable nOPV2 vaccine, which has been administered to over 143.6 million children in Nigeria [ , , ], enhancing routine immunization, with the aim of maintaining poliovirus immunity and preventing cVDPV2 outbreaks [ , ]. This review aimed to identify existing policies, strategies and interventions for polio eradication in Nigeria and their impact on polio vaccine uptake and eradication efforts in the country. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Search Strategy An adapted systematic literature review was conducted in April 2024 using Ovid Medline and PubMed databases, which are the world’s leading bibliographic sources for biomedical and life sciences scholarly literature and research resources with the aim of improving health globally [ , ], alongside gray literature from Google Scholar not indexed in the Ovid Medline and PubMed databases, to identify articles reporting on the impact of polio vaccination services, compliance with immunization schedules, vaccine hesitancy and utilization of intervention policies directed towards polio eradication in Nigeria (see ). Two databases were considered for the literature search to ensure comprehensive coverage of relevant articles [ , ]. Both published and gray literature were included to enhance the evidence base and minimize the impact of publication bias, which can occur when mainly research studies with statistically significant findings are published, as compared to less statistically significant results [ ]. Potential limitations of the search strategy are documented in . Box 1. Limitations of search strategy Exclusion of literature (n = 261) focusing on subgroups or unrelated disease conditions and interventions. For example, the impact of COVID-19 on polio eradication services was excluded. Limiting the search to articles written in English. The present study excluded research published in other languages. Reliance on specific keywords in the PICO framework might miss articles that use different terminology or synonyms not included in the search terms. The search was focused on studies from 2018 to 2023; the study required comprehensive searches and adequate data from previous years, before 2018, ensuring that the study was based on recent and relevant research, which is in line with current evidence, practices and policies across the years. Some aspects of the PICO framework such as the “study design concept” were not relevant to the search strategy as the study is an exploratory, single-intervention study. The review followed the key principles of systematic reviews, with literature identified using the most recent 2020 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Flowchart relating to database searches and the inclusion/exclusion process [ ]. Search strategies used the Population, Intervention, Comparator and Outcome (PICO) framework [ ] ( ) to define key concepts, MeSH terms, MeSH tree subheadings and free search terms. 2.2. Selection Criteria Inclusion and exclusion criteria were identified prior to conducting the search to reduce the risk of selection bias. Eligibility criteria included articles published in English after 2018, to ensure that the study was based on the most recent and relevant evidence, which is in line with current practices, policies and recommendations. The following search terms were used: “Impact”, “Polio”, “Nigeria”, “Polio vaccination services”, “Polio intervention policies” and “vaccine hesitancy’’, with the Ovid Medline and PubMed searches available in . News or commentary articles were excluded. Full search Strategies for Pubmed literatures showing MeSH and free search terms generated for each PICO/S CONCEPT are available from the authors. 2.3. Data Extraction and Analysis/Synthesis Data extraction and synthesis were conducted by OE using an Excel spreadsheet and discussed with SC. Themes were identified by thematic analysis of key issues across the 26 studies, using a synthesis table to represent central topics or subjects from the data sources. The quality of the evidence in each study was assessed and appraised using the adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Program (CASP) [ ]. The evidence summary table was modified from the Public Health Agency of Canada’s Control Guidelines Critical Appraisal Tool Kit [ ]. 3. Results Six key themes were identified from the 26 studies included in the review: (1) polio intervention policies and programs; (2) polio vaccination services and mass campaigns; (3) vaccine uptake and vaccine hesitancy; (4) the Nigerian health system; (5) surveillance monitoring systems for polio eradication; and (6) challenges of polio vaccination services and interventions in terms of their impact on eradication efforts in Nigeria. 3.1. Polio Intervention Policies and Programs summarizes the polio intervention policies and programs identified in Nigeria. The Polio Eradication Initiative (PEI) enhanced health promotion, maternal and child health interventions, health worker skills, resource development, service delivery and system efficiency in health programs [ ]. This included Emergency Operation Centers (EOCs) and improved data management systems, which supported the broader health system during outbreaks [ ]. However, applying the PEI in a weak and understaffed health system led to role-shifting, reducing human resources efforts in rural areas and impacting service delivery [ ]. Community engagement activities were important in Nigeria’s PEI as well as the need for well-structured implementation and continuous monitoring to ensure the effectiveness and sustainability of community engagement strategies [ ]. The National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) and Data Working Group (DWG) were found to have played a crucial role in the Nigerian Polio Eradication Program [ , ], reducing the number of WPV1 cases from 122 in 2012 to zero by 2015, and enhancing its capabilities for managing other outbreaks like Ebola, measles, yellow fever and meningitis [ ]. EOCs had enhanced coordination, strategic direction and disease control initiatives, but required significant financial support to maintain their functions [ ]. The DWG provided quality surveillance and campaign information and assessed the preparedness for OPV SIAs. Independent monitoring and Lot Quality Assurance Sampling surveys identified low-performing areas for revaccination, with the data enabling the NEOC to make evidence-based decisions, identify gaps, improve preparedness and enhance routine immunization and surveillance activities [ ]. The National Stop Transmission of Polio Program’s immunization program and eradication efforts contributed to improved immunization services in Nigeria, particularly in underserved areas [ ], emphasizing the importance of targeted supervision and pre-campaign planning to enhance health campaign outcomes in regions with weak health campaigns [ ]. The Core Group Partners Project (CGPP) and Volunteer Community Mobilizers (VCMs), introduced in Nigeria in 2014 to address the health and safety concerns of the northern communities, enhanced community engagement, helping to identify at risk groups and regions and improving polio vaccine acceptance [ , , ]. Through the CGPP initiative, the number of WPV cases in Nigeria decreased from 1122 in 2006 to only 6 WPV cases in 2014 [ , , ]. The training and empowerment of local volunteers highlighted the importance of community involvement and capacity building in public health systems, as VCMs improved vaccine acceptance by addressing community-specific concerns [ , ]. However, challenges included community resistance, misinformation, logistical challenges and security issues in high-risk areas [ ]. The Nigerian government established the NPI with the primary goal of supporting the implementation of state and local government area immunization programs and providing free routine immunization [ , ]. In addition, the WHO, in collaboration with other partners such as the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, supported routine polio immunization, resulting in improved access to and coverage of routine immunization services [ ]. The Nigerian NPI has, however, fallen short of achieving its goals due to inadequate infrastructure, lack of funding and poor service delivery, which have recently been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic [ , ]. Nigeria’s polio eradication efforts were aided by international collaborations and partnerships. The WHO, through its transition framework, provided a comprehensive assessment of collaborative strategies emphasizing the importance of local and international partnerships with other countries and agencies, including, but not limited to, the WHO, UNICEF and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation [ ]. Effective global collaboration transferred necessary resources and funding in support of polio eradication efforts and secured ongoing international commitment to assistance [ ]. The WHO also provided vital insights into Nigeria’s polio transition plan to safeguard the essential polio functions, including poliovirus surveillance, immunization with appropriate polio vaccines, outbreak response and eradication efforts [ ]. 3.2. Extensive vaccination campaigns and high coverage of polio vaccination significantly reduced the incidence and eventually eliminated wild poliovirus in Nigeria. In 2020, Nigeria was declared free of wild poliovirus [ ], with a 30% increase in polio vaccination rates, attributed to targeted vaccination services [ , ]. Polio Vaccination Services: Frequency of Mass Campaigns and Immunization Coverage Conflicting evidence was found on the impact of polio vaccination services providing frequent mass campaigns and immunization to boost polio eradication efforts in Nigeria. Extensive vaccination campaigns and high coverage of polio vaccination significantly reduced the incidence and eventually eliminated wild poliovirus in Nigeria. In 2020, Nigeria was declared free of wild poliovirus [ ], with a 30% increase in polio vaccination rates, attributed to targeted vaccination services [ , ]. Community health workers played pivotal roles in increasing vaccine acceptance and coverage in local communities [ , ]. Other papers have emphasized the importance of community engagement and trust in the success of vaccination campaigns as data indicate a substantial increase in vaccination coverage in Northern and Southern Nigeria, especially in Northern Nigeria, where community engagement was previously low but rose from 45% in 2010 to 85% in 2020 [ , ]. However, integrating mass polio campaigns with routine health services in weaker health systems can divert resources away from other health programs, which frequently results in a lack of attention to basic health services and increased workload for healthcare workers [ , ]. Moreover, while mass vaccination campaigns and health systems through PEI implementation boosted health promotion activities and improved coverage for maternal and child health interventions [ ], implementation within a weak health system causes a shift in health workers’ primary roles towards polio with potential neglect of other health programs due to resource diversion [ , , ]. 3.3. Vaccine Coverage and Vaccine Hesitancy Attempts to eradicate polio in Nigeria have been significantly influenced by both coverage of vaccine schedules and vaccine hesitancy. Mass immunization campaigns increased the uptake of vaccines and including polio vaccination into routine immunization schedules significantly improved coverage, helping to sustain high immunization coverage over time [ ]. Moreover, National Immunization Days effectively boosted immunization rates and compliance [ , ], and decreased polio cases due to higher vaccination compliance [ , ]. In January 2019, the WHO declared vaccine hesitancy as one of the top 10 leading threats to global public health [ ]. In Nigeria, vaccine hesitancy due to cultural and religious beliefs and practices has been a significant factor influencing vaccination decisions. Cultural beliefs, misinformation and distrust in Western medicine were identified as reasons for vaccine hesitancy, especially in Northern Nigeria, which has hindered vaccination efforts [ , , ]. Contrary to evidence about the success of mass immunization campaigns, there was also evidence of the unintended consequences of frequent campaigns, contributing to increased vaccine hesitancy in some communities. Some people felt overwhelmed by frequent campaigns, leading to a decrease in community participation, straining available resources in already weak health systems and resulting in lack of motivation among health workers [ ]. 3.4. The Nigerian Healthcare System The co-delivery of polio vaccination services with other health interventions and services improved overall health outcomes and vaccination rates [ , , ]. Integrating polio campaigns with other health services is important in helping to prevent the negative effects of frequent campaigns in a weak healthcare system and promoting community acceptance [ , ]. While initially a more focused approach to polio-specific activities, without integration with other health services, was advocated for [ ], others have reported that the integration of other health services into polio eradication efforts ensured that health systems could respond more effectively to public health needs, improve vaccination uptake rates and enhance overall health service delivery [ , ]. Evidence showed that high-intensity immunization campaigns can cause fatigue, reduce motivation among health workers and also reduce community participation [ , , ]. However, another study supports mass vaccination campaigns involving non-governmental organizations and volunteer community mobilizers as being cost-effective in high-risk areas [ ]. Furthermore, modeling has shown that increasing the number of SIA rounds significantly reduced cVDPV cases, if effectively managed [ ]. 3.5. Surveillance Monitoring Systems in Polio Eradication Efforts The National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) and Data Working Group (DWG) were responsible for the monitoring of and campaign information for the Nigerian Polio Eradication Program from 2016 to 2020 [ ]. The NEOC used a pre-campaign dashboard to assess preparedness for supplementary immunization activities, for example, the use of acute flaccid paralysis surveillance data for case–control studies, with additional community controls surveyed from April 2021 [ , ]. Data indicated that >95% of children with non-polio acute flaccid paralysis had received >3 doses of OPV, highlighting high immunization coverage [ , ]. Active surveillance of adverse events of special interest was used to monitor the safety of nOPV2 in Nigeria [ ]. Challenges to Polio Vaccination Services and Eradication Efforts in Nigeria There have been various barriers to polio vaccination and eradication programs, emphasizing the importance of considering local contexts, community trust and effective communication in program implementation [ ]. Barriers included a fear of vaccine side effects, distrust in the government and health services, poor infrastructure, negative cultural and religious beliefs and geopolitical instability [ ]. Lack of resources and funding has impacted negatively on immunization coverage in Nigeria, as the general lack of basic necessities, including shortages of vaccines and supplies, instability of the cold chain, lack of training for health workers and volunteers, cancellation of immunization schedules and insecurity were identified as possible reasons for low coverage [ ]. The WHO has reported a funding gap of US 132 million for effective polio eradication functions in Nigeria [ ]. A report of the Center for Disease Control (CDC) reflected that from 2016 to 2017, there was an 87% reduction in the number of children in Nigeria without access to poliovirus vaccination compared to <60% in terms of national poliovirus vaccine coverage levels through routine immunization services since 2002 [ ]. On the other hand, another study reported that the country experienced a setback in 2016 due to insecurity in northeastern Nigeria that started in 2012, restricting surveillance, immunization coverage and detection of WPV transmission, resulting in a resurgence of endemic WPV transmission in 2016 [ ]. Over 60 polio campaigns were suspended by the GPEI during the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in an increase in cases of cVDPV2 and outbreaks of cVDPV1 [ ]. Evidently, COVID-19 caused gaps in polio detection and monitoring, and damaged health systems more broadly, including essential immunization programs. 4. Discussion and Future Directions This review identified and assessed the impact of polio intervention services and policies on polio vaccine uptake and eradication efforts in Nigeria. summarizes the key issues associated with low polio uptake that were identified in this paper, together with recommendations for changes to practice and policy to improve polio vaccination uptake in Nigeria and globally and recommendations for addressing these barriers in the short-term (1–2 years), mid-term (3–4 years) and long-term (5+ years). While the recommendations relate to improving polio uptake in Nigeria, they have transferable learning globally for all vaccination programs. 4.1. The Burden of Polio Globally and in Nigeria The burden of WPV globally has fallen by 99%, from an estimated 350,000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries in 1988 to 12 cases in two endemic countries (Pakistan and Afghanistan) in August 2024, largely due to the efforts of the GPEI [ , ]. However, continued reports of cases of cVDPV in 2024 in Nigeria and the recent outbreak and re-emergence of paralytic polio in Gaza after 25 years show that if circumstances disrupt routine immunization, and there is a deterioration in hygiene and sanitation in any country, there is a risk of the highly infectious poliovirus thriving in that region, as it can easily be imported and spread within a polio-free country [ ]. Moreover, while WPV has been successfully eradicated in Nigeria, there are ongoing risks for Nigeria with respect to both type 1 and type 3 vaccine-derived poliovirus outbreaks [ ]. An outbreak of the type 1 virus in Nigeria could prolong interruption of the transmission of the VDPV by an extended period, and could pose a continuing threat to public health in Nigeria and other countries through international spread [ ]. To reduce the burden of polio in Nigeria in the short-term, it is imperative to enhance immunization campaigns via SIAs, both generally and, in particular, in high-risk areas with low vaccination coverage and a high burden of polio, using the genetically stable nOPV2 to quickly control outbreaks of VDPV, as recommended by the Global nOPV2 Advisory Group [ , ]. There is a need to strengthen effective surveillance systems to improve early detection of poliovirus; for example, digital health tools can be used for real-time data collection and response, especially in hard-to-reach areas [ , ]. There is a need to strengthen effective surveillance systems to improve early detection of poliovirus; for example, digital health tools can be used for real-time data collection and response, especially in hard-to-reach areas [ , ]. The reduction in polio cases from 2006 to 2014 shows the impact of surveillance systems in reaching unvaccinated populations and preventing resurgence of WPV [ , , , ]. The COVID-19 vaccine rollout demonstrated the need and opportunity to improve pharmacovigilance by integrating national vaccine platforms with surveillance across the African continent [ ]. Community groups can encourage vaccine uptake by engaging community members to participate in local health campaigns and immunization programs [ , ]. The WHO vaccine advisory group recommended that community health workers and religious and community leaders can help address cultural concerns and misinformation about vaccines to encourage vaccine acceptance [ ]. Neel et al. [ ] observed similar reductions in polio cases in Ethiopia and India through high-coverage campaigns by community health workers. In the medium term, there is a need to increase routine immunization coverage to reduce the polio burden in low vaccinated areas, necessitating an expansion of the vaccine supply to ensure full vaccination coverage and to ensure that routine immunization programs reach at least 90% of <5 year-old children [ ]. This will require improvements to health system and workforce infrastructure in Nigeria to minimize the risk of infectious diseases and to reduce disease burden over time [ ]. Increasing healthcare service funding and utilizing the public–private partnership (PPP) model, targeting non-profit, private and government partnerships that promote polio intervention services, could reduce the burden of polio in Nigeria [ ]. There is also a need to monitor and contain cross-border transmission by cross-border surveillance and collaborative immunization campaigns between neighboring countries to prevent the spread of poliovirus across borders [ ]. This review has found that sustained planning is required to embed improvements, with long-term recommendations including the need to maintain high immunization coverage and the development of policies that enhance the effectiveness of mass campaigns and promote the integration of campaign strategies with routine health services, thereby reducing the polio burden [ ]. Such long-term planning requires the retention of polio eradication infrastructure and strategies to re-use various polio response frameworks to maintain preparedness for infectious disease outbreaks; for instance, the polio National Emergency Operation Centers (EOCs) could be transitioned to support broader public health functions [ ]. Funding would need to be sustained both in Nigeria and globally, with global collaborative funding to combat infectious diseases as well as ongoing surveillance and disease response activities [ , ]. Evidence from Afghanistan and Pakistan shows that collaboration with neighboring countries has reduced WPV burden across borders [ ]. Finally, there is a need for further and ongoing research to explore the impact of the burden of polio and other infectious diseases on health systems [ ]; for example, to support the continued use of nOPV2 to reduce the burden of polio [ ]. 4.2. Existing Policies, Strategies and Interventions and Their Impact on Polio Eradication in Nigeria Polio policies, frameworks and strategic plans ( ) have impacted polio eradication efforts and enhanced public health outcomes in Nigeria. For instance, the WHO Polio Transition Plan outlined strategies for integrating polio activities into the Nigerian health system with respect to the eradication of all forms of polio in Nigeria [ , , ]. Similarly, the GPEI strategies were pivotal in reducing WPV transmission [ ], while the introduction of the National Polio Emergency Action Plan, routine immunization policies and SIAs significantly enhanced the incorporation of polio vaccination services into routine immunization schedules and improved integration with routine health services [ , , ]. Collaborative partnerships have supported the polio eradication efforts of the Nigerian government and, for example, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the WHO, the CDC, UNICEF, Gavi and Rotary International, boosting the confidence of the public with respect to vaccinations and mobilizing resources and funding for mass immunization campaigns, surveillance activities and coordination of eradication efforts [ ]. Evidence from interventions in polio-endemic regions like Afghanistan and Pakistan shows that collaboration with GPEI partners and neighboring countries, augmented by community engagement and capacity building, has been important in preventing the spread of wild poliovirus across borders. But such efforts require regional collaboration from other countries in the provision of resources, funding and advocacy with respect to the eradication of polio in all affected countries [ , , ]. But such efforts require regional collaboration from other countries in the provision of resources, funding and advocacy with respect to the eradication of polio in all affected countries [ , , ]. Routine vaccination programs and National Immunization Days increased the uptake of vaccines and improved polio eradication efforts [ , ], with vaccine compliance reducing polio incidence and improving broader health outcomes by preventing other vaccine-preventable diseases through integrated health services [ ]. Vaccine hesitancy, one of the WHO’s top ten threats to global public health [ ], along with a polio vaccine boycott, undermined polio intervention policies and immunization coverage, especially in Northern Nigeria [ ], which posed challenges in terms of maintaining population immunity against poliovirus [ ]. Community-based intervention groups such as VCMs and the CGPP utilized community engagement strategies to help to improve vaccination uptake and address health safety acceptance, demonstrating the critical role of culturally sensitive approaches in public health interventions [ , , ]. Community participation in mobilizing community members to participate in intervention programs is integral to promoting vaccine compliance and acceptance of intervention programs. [ , ]. However, vaccine hesitancy remains a significant barrier to the successful eradication of polio in Nigeria and is the major contributory factor to the re-emergence of cVDPV2 [ ], underpinned by multiple complex contributors, including cultural, religious, security and political factors, particularly in Northern Nigeria [ , , ]. Other factors, relating to the WHO SAGE Working Group 3C (convenience, complacency and confidence) model of vaccine hesitancy [ ], included insecurity in hard-to-reach areas, lack of funding, government ownership, low motivation among health workers and poor resource management [ , , ], as well as community resistance, misinformation, population displacement due to conflicts and variations in data collection [ ]. Addressing misinformation and vaccine hesitancy is crucial for the success of vaccination programs, and ensuring high coverage of vaccinations to achieve herd immunity is essential [ ]. Effective engagement of communities and education about the safety of vaccines are required to promote vaccine acceptance and to overcome cultural and informational challenges that contribute to vaccine hesitancy [ , ]. The delivery of polio intervention services in conjunction with other healthcare services within the broader health system can also improve overall health outcomes [ , , ] and help health systems improve vaccination rates and other public health services [ , ]. For example, co-delivery of healthcare services such as distribution of treated mosquito nets and Vitamin A supplements to nursing mothers with other polio vaccination services promoted community participation and acceptance of intervention, as recommended by the WHO [ , ]. However, frequent mass vaccination campaigns can increase health workers’ workload and result in fatigue if not effectively integrated with broader health services [ , ]. An overwhelming focus on polio eradication has the potential of straining health system infrastructure and diverting resources away from other health services [ , , ]; for example, limiting vaccination coverage and the health system’s capacity to respond to other health emergencies in Afghanistan and Pakistan [ ]. The COVID-19 pandemic affected Nigeria’s polio eradication programs and highlighted limitations and weaknesses in the healthcare system [ ]. For example, the COVID-19 vaccine rollout coincided with responses to the cVDPV2 outbreak. State-level resources were insufficient to oversee polio outbreak response campaigns and maintain cold-chain systems in the different states, with vaccination teams unable to reach some eligible children under 5 years of age in remote areas—a situation aggravated by ongoing security threats due to the insurgency in Nigeria [ , ]. In addition, the monopoly on distribution of nOPV2 by a single manufacturer delayed some vaccine distribution to Nigeria [ ]. 5. Conclusions The aim of this review was to evaluate the impact of polio intervention services and policies on polio vaccine uptake and eradication efforts in Nigeria, which, after years of multi-sectoral polio eradication efforts, eradicated WPV in 2020. Nigeria has one of the highest burdens of VDPV from genetic mutation of the type 2 component of OPV, which has caused transmission of cVDPV2, particularly in communities with low immunity and poor immunization coverage [ ]. The persistence of cVDPV2 is aggravated by vaccine hesitancy caused by cultural and religious influences, insecurity and poor health infrastructure. Despite the public health success of vaccination generally, building public confidence in vaccines and improving systems to monitor safety while maintaining data security and patient privacy are essential [ ]. This review has identified progress made through mass immunization campaigns, integration of polio intervention services into the broader health system, targeted community engagement and international collaboration to facilitate polio eradication strategies. However, multiple reasons have been identified for low or delayed polio vaccine uptake and the resulting challenges with global polio eradication, which adversely impact the control and eradication of infectious and communicable diseases such as polio [ , , ]. These challenges involve a complex interplay of factors, including misconceptions and misunderstandings about the polio vaccine; lack of access to healthcare services; a boycott in Northern Nigeria and vaccine hesitancy; illiteracy; areas in conflict, such as the area affected by the Boko Haram insurgency; challenges in reaching underserved communities; an ineffective vaccine service delivery system; deficits in surveillance and monitoring systems; low motivation among health workers; poor resource management and failures in the cold-chain system that have affected the delivery of vaccines in Nigeria; and, more recently, the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, which disrupted global polio vaccination campaigns [ , , , , , , ]. These experiences emphasize the need for healthcare system strengthening [ ] and a sustained and funded focus on quality driven healthcare [ ]. Also needed is a parallel focus on long-term workforce planning [ ] and improved coordination at the national level among regulatory authorities and the department of health. Results from this review have important implications for public health practice and policy, both in Nigeria and globally. The recommendations and research priorities that have been suggested offer strategic advice for policymakers, researchers, public health professionals and clinical practitioners with respect to addressing the identified gaps and challenges. If implemented, the advice arising from this study would enhance the opportunities for Nigeria to sustain its WPD-free status and eradicate all variant forms of polio.
